sections.Overview:
Definition

An acromioclavicular joint injury is damage to the ligamentous and capsular stabilisers connecting the distal clavicle to the acromion, commonly caused by direct impact to the superior or lateral shoulder. The term “shoulder separation” is often used; it is distinct from a glenohumeral dislocation.1

Also known as

ACJ sprain, ACJ separation, ACJ dislocation, shoulder separation.

Classification or grading

  • Rockwood I: AC ligament sprain; AC and CC alignment preserved; no radiographic displacement.
  • Rockwood II: AC ligament disruption with CC ligament sprain; mild clavicular elevation and widening of the AC interval.
  • Rockwood III: complete AC and CC ligament disruption; distal clavicle displaced superiorly, conventionally 25–100% increase in CC distance versus the opposite side.
  • Rockwood IV: distal clavicle displaced posteriorly into or through the trapezius.
  • Rockwood V: marked superior displacement with extensive disruption of the deltotrapezial fascia; CC distance conventionally increased 100–300%.
  • Rockwood VI: distal clavicle displaced inferiorly, beneath the acromion or coracoid region; rare.

Types IV–VI are generally referred for orthopaedic assessment and usually considered operative injuries. Type III is controversial and is not automatically an indication for surgery.1,2

Three-point summary

  1. Establish whether the presentation is an acute traumatic ACJ injury and exclude fracture, neurovascular injury and associated shoulder pathology.
  2. Use clinical findings plus appropriate radiographs to classify displacement; no single special test establishes the diagnosis.
  3. Most low-grade injuries and many type III injuries are managed non-operatively with symptom-guided protection and progressive rehabilitation.2,3
sections.Epidemiology & risk factors:
Prevalence and incidence

A prospective Oslo cohort recorded ACJ injuries as 11% of all shoulder injuries and an incidence of 45 per 100,000 person-years. Sports accounted for 53% of ACJ injuries in that cohort. These estimates are setting-specific and should not be treated as Australian population rates.3 A review reports that ACJ injuries are common in contact sports, but sport-specific rates vary substantially by sport, cohort and case definition.1

Typical patient

Often a young adult involved in contact or collision sport, cycling, skiing or a fall directly onto the shoulder. The Oslo cohort was predominantly male, with the highest frequency in men in their twenties.3

Modifiable risk factors

  • Exposure to collision sport, falls and high-risk cycling environments is modifiable at an exposure level; evidence for individual conditioning as a primary prevention strategy is insufficient.
  • Protective equipment and sport-specific risk-reduction strategies may reduce impact exposure, but ACJ-specific preventive effectiveness is not established.

Non-modifiable risk factors

  • Age and sex associations are reported epidemiologically; they are not deterministic predictors for an individual.
  • Previous injury and residual instability may influence subsequent loading tolerance, but the magnitude of risk is not established by the sources reviewed here.

sections.Pathoanatomy & mechanism:
Structures involved

  • AC capsuloligamentous complex: superior, inferior, anterior and posterior AC ligament components; the superior and posterior capsular structures contribute importantly to horizontal stability.
  • Coracoclavicular (CC) ligaments: conoid (more medial/posterior) and trapezoid (more lateral/anterior); together they provide major vertical restraint between clavicle and coracoid.
  • Deltotrapezial fascia: contributes to dynamic and soft-tissue restraint; more extensive stripping is associated with high-grade injuries, particularly type V.
  • Intra-articular disc: fibrocartilaginous structure that may degenerate or become damaged; its specific contribution to acute Rockwood grading is not a primary grading criterion.

Mechanism of injury or onset

Typically a direct blow to the superolateral shoulder with the arm adducted, driving the acromion inferiorly relative to the clavicle. A fall onto an outstretched hand can also transmit force to the ACJ. Repetitive loading may produce distal clavicle osteolysis, which is a differential rather than an acute ligament separation.1,2

Pathophysiology

Injury severity reflects the structures disrupted and direction/magnitude of clavicular displacement. AC ligament failure compromises horizontal restraint; CC ligament failure increases vertical displacement. Higher-grade trauma may detach the deltoid and trapezius fascia and produce posterior or inferior displacement patterns.1,2

Natural history

Low-grade injuries generally settle with non-operative care. A visible prominence may remain after ligament disruption even when pain and function improve. Some people experience persistent pain, scapular dyskinesis or symptomatic horizontal/vertical instability; structural appearance alone does not establish functional failure. Evidence on the proportion with persistent symptoms is heterogeneous.2,4
sections.Clinical presentation:
Area and nature of symptoms

Localised pain and tenderness over the ACJ at the top of the shoulder, sometimes with swelling, bruising or a visible step deformity. Pain may refer into the lateral shoulder but should prompt consideration of other sources if it extends below the elbow or is accompanied by neurological symptoms.

Aggravating and easing factors

  • Aggravated by direct pressure (lying on the affected side, backpack straps), cross-body adduction, pushing, lifting, bench press, overhead activity and contact.
  • Often eased by supporting the arm, relative rest, appropriate analgesia and temporarily reducing compressive or heavy upper-limb loading.

24-hour pattern

Acute pain may be present at rest and disturb sleep, particularly when rolling onto the affected side. A consistent ACJ-specific diurnal pattern is not established; ask about night pain, sleep position and response to activity.

Irritability (SIN)

Severity, irritability and nature are assessed individually. High irritability is suggested by marked pain at rest, pronounced tenderness, pain with small movements and difficulty tolerating examination. Do not infer Rockwood grade from pain intensity.

Functional limitations

  • Dressing, washing hair, reaching across the body and carrying a bag.
  • Pushing up from a chair, push-ups, bench press, lifting, throwing and overhead work.
  • Contact sport, falling onto the shoulder and sleeping on the involved side.
sections.Differential diagnosis:
Red flags for this presentation

  • Urgent assessment: open injury, skin tenting or threatened skin over a markedly displaced clavicle, suspected fracture, gross deformity, or suspected posterior/inferior displacement.
  • Emergency: absent or reduced distal pulses, cool/pale hand, progressive paraesthesia or motor deficit, expanding haematoma, chest pain or respiratory compromise after significant trauma.
  • Consider infection, malignancy or systemic disease where there is fever, unexplained constitutional symptoms, non-traumatic progressive pain or relevant history.

sections.Subjective examination:
Patient goals and expectations

  • Clarify desired activities: work demands, dominant arm, lifting, overhead tasks, contact sport, competition level and target return date.
  • Ask what the patient understands about the visible prominence and whether cosmesis is a major concern.
  • Establish previous shoulder injury, instability, surgery, relevant medical history, analgesia, occupation and current training load.
  • Clarify mechanism, exact point of impact, immediate function, swelling/bruising and whether there was a transient deformity.

Psychosocial screen

Explore fear of movement or re-injury, confidence in the shoulder, sleep, mood, work/financial pressures, sport selection pressure and expectations of surgery. Ask whether the patient is avoiding movement because of pain, fear or advice received. Use shared decision-making and avoid implying that a radiographic deformity necessarily means poor function.

sections.Objective examination:
Observation

  • Inspect from anterior, lateral and posterior views for swelling, bruising, skin integrity, step deformity and clavicular prominence.
  • Compare both shoulders; observe resting scapular position and scapular movement during elevation and lowering.
  • Look for skin tenting, threatened skin or gross displacement and refer urgently where present.

Range of motion

Assess cervical and shoulder active range first, within irritability. Record flexion, abduction, external and internal rotation and cross-body reach. Compare sides and note pain location, range and movement strategy. Use passive range only when appropriate; avoid forceful end-range compression in an acutely irritable injury.

Strength testing

Assess isometric shoulder flexion, abduction, internal/external rotation, elbow and grip as tolerated. Distinguish pain inhibition from true weakness. In significant trauma, assess deltoid and cuff function without stressing an unstable joint.

Neurological screen

Screen upper-limb sensation, myotomes and reflexes when indicated; check distal pulses, capillary refill, hand temperature and colour after significant trauma or where symptoms suggest neurovascular compromise.

Functional tests

Progress from hand-to-head and hand-behind-back to controlled reaching, wall push, lifting and task-specific tests as symptoms permit. Do not perform provocative contact or maximal strength tests in an acute high-grade injury.

Special tests and diagnostic accuracy

Accuracy estimates below come from different populations and reference standards. Chronic surgical cohorts and non-traumatic primary-care cohorts do not directly represent acute traumatic separation. Interpret results in context.

sections.Imaging & investigations:
Decision rule for imaging

There is no universally validated physiotherapy decision rule specific to ACJ separation. Following significant direct trauma, deformity, focal bony tenderness, substantial loss of function or suspected high-grade injury, obtain medical assessment and radiographs to classify the injury and exclude fracture. Do not use a normal special test to rule out structural injury.

Preferred modality

  • Plain radiographs: initial investigation. Typical views include AP and bilateral comparison/Zanca views; an axillary view can help assess posterior displacement. Compare CC distance with the contralateral side when appropriate.
  • Weighted/stress views: not recommended routinely. An older paired-radiograph study found that weights rarely revealed a higher grade not visible on standard films; this is old evidence and contemporary practice varies.[verify: DOI and full citation for weighted-view study]
  • CT: consider where complex bony injury or displacement requires definition.
  • MRI: may clarify ligament, deltotrapezial fascia or associated soft-tissue injury when it will change management; not routinely required for straightforward cases.
  • Ultrasound: may assess superficial structures or guide diagnostic injection in selected chronic pain cases, but is not the standard method for Rockwood grading.

When to refer on

  • Urgent emergency/orthopaedic assessment for open injury, threatened skin, neurovascular compromise, suspected posterior/inferior displacement, fracture or major associated injury.
  • Orthopaedic assessment for suspected Rockwood IV–VI, substantial displacement, diagnostic uncertainty or persistent functional limitation.
  • Consider specialist review for type III where high-demand occupational/sport requirements, persistent symptoms after an adequate rehabilitation trial or patient preference make operative discussion relevant.

sections.Management:
Management depends on injury grade, skin/neurovascular status, symptoms, functional demands and patient preference. The dosing below is a pragmatic symptom-guided framework, not a validated universal protocol; ACJ-specific rehabilitation trials are scarce.8

InterventionRecommendationDetail
Sling / early protectionConditionalShort-term sling for comfort in acute painful injuries; remove regularly for elbow, wrist and hand movement. Wean as pain settles and active movement improves. Avoid prolonged immobilisation without a clear reason.
AnalgesiaConditionalDiscuss simple analgesia or NSAIDs with a pharmacist/medical practitioner where appropriate, considering contraindications and individual risk. Medication prescribing is outside physiotherapy scope unless separately authorised.
Early shoulder movementRecommendedBegin comfortable pendulum/table-supported movement and pain-limited active-assisted elevation when tolerated. Avoid forceful cross-body adduction and heavy loading early.
Scapular controlRecommendedStart low-load scapular setting/retraction and supported control drills, for example 2–3 sets of 8–15 repetitions, once tolerated. Progress range and resistance without increasing symptoms the following day.
Rotator cuff strengtheningRecommendedBegin submaximal isometric external/internal rotation with elbow by side; progress to light band resistance, commonly 2–3 sets of 8–15 repetitions, 2–3 days/week. Adjust dose to irritability; no ACJ-specific optimal dose has been established.

sections.Education & self-management:
Key messages

  • “You have injured the joint between your collarbone and shoulder blade. The pain can be significant, but pain does not tell us exactly how severe the ligament injury is.”
  • “The small bump may remain because the collarbone can sit higher after the ligaments are injured. The bump does not automatically mean your shoulder will stay weak or painful.”
  • “Our goal is to get your shoulder moving and strong enough for the things you need to do, not necessarily to make the X-ray or appearance look normal.”
  • “We will protect it while it is irritable, then build the load back up in stages. Some discomfort can occur, but a marked flare that lasts into the next day means we should adjust the dose.”

Load and activity advice

Temporarily reduce direct pressure, heavy pushing/pulling, cross-body loading, overhead lifting and contact exposure. Maintain lower-limb and cardiovascular exercise where safe. Use a comfortable sleep position and avoid lying directly on the injured shoulder while irritable. Return to work with modified duties where possible rather than assuming complete work absence is required.

Self-management plan

  1. Use sling only as needed for comfort and follow the treating clinician's advice about weaning.
  2. Maintain hand, wrist and elbow movement; perform prescribed comfortable shoulder movement.
  3. Complete the agreed scapular and cuff programme at the prescribed frequency.
  4. Track pain, sleep, movement and next-day response; reduce load if symptoms progressively worsen.
  5. Progress lifting, pushing, overhead tasks and sport-specific drills only when the current stage is tolerated.
  6. Seek urgent review for new hand colour/temperature change, altered sensation, progressive weakness, skin compromise or rapidly worsening symptoms.
sections.Medical & surgical management:
When to refer

Refer urgently for neurovascular compromise, threatened skin, open injury, suspected fracture or posterior/inferior displacement. Refer to an orthopaedic shoulder specialist for high-grade injuries, uncertain classification, substantial displacement or persistent pain/instability despite rehabilitation.

Medical options

Medical management may include analgesia, short-term anti-inflammatory medication where appropriate, radiographic assessment and review of associated injuries. A diagnostic local anaesthetic injection can be considered by an appropriately trained medical practitioner for persistent focal ACJ pain when diagnosis remains uncertain. Injection is not a substitute for acute injury assessment.

Surgical options and post-op protocol

Procedures include fixation/reduction constructs and anatomical CC ligament reconstruction, sometimes with AC capsular repair. Choice depends on injury pattern, chronicity, surgeon expertise and patient goals. Hook plates require planned removal in many protocols and have implant-related complications; contemporary reconstruction techniques vary.

Type III operative versus non-operative evidence

A multicentre randomised trial of acute type III injuries found no clinically important functional advantage for surgery at follow-up; surgery improved radiographic alignment but was associated with more complications and slower early recovery in some outcomes.9 A separate randomised trial including type III and V injuries found better early outcomes in the non-operative groups and no significant functional difference at later follow-up; 18% of participants allocated to non-operative care later underwent surgery.4 These findings support offering non-operative care to many type III patients, while recognising individual high-demand or persistently symptomatic cases may require specialist discussion.

Post-operative phases

  • Protection: sling/brace and restricted shoulder movement according to the specific reconstruction and surgeon instructions. Protect the repair; maintain hand, wrist and elbow movement.
  • Early movement: introduce passive or assisted ROM only within surgeon-defined limits; avoid loading, cross-body stress and unsupported lifting while repair is vulnerable.
  • Restore ROM and control: progress active-assisted to active movement when cleared; begin gentle scapular and cuff activation as permitted.
  • Strength and function: progress resistance and closed-chain loading after clearance and adequate healing; then integrate work- and sport-specific tasks.
  • Return to contact: only after surgeon clearance, healed repair, full functional ROM, adequate strength and successful graded contact preparation. Protocols vary substantially; a review of published protocols found return-to-sport recommendations spanning 12–48 weeks, demonstrating that a single universal timeline is not defensible.10
sections.Prognosis:
Expected timeframes

Recovery varies by Rockwood grade, associated injury, irritability, occupation and sport demands. Low-grade injuries often improve over several weeks; type III injuries may require a longer rehabilitation period. These are broad clinical expectations rather than validated individual predictions. The best available controlled data should be interpreted in light of the study population and surgical technique.

Factors linked to better or worse outcomes

  • Potentially favourable: lower-grade injury, improving pain and ROM, progressive loading tolerance, confidence and ability to modify work/sport temporarily.
  • Potentially unfavourable: high-grade displacement, associated fracture or soft-tissue injury, persistent instability, ongoing pain, high physical job demands and fear/apprehension.
  • Radiographic prominence may persist despite good function; appearance and disability are not interchangeable.

Return to previous sport and residual symptoms

A reliable ACJ-specific proportion returning to the exact pre-injury sport level and a robust estimate of residual symptoms at one year were not established from the controlled sources reviewed. Cosmetic prominence, local discomfort, fatigue, scapular dyskinesis or symptoms with heavy cross-body loading may persist in some people; the frequency should not be stated as a precise percentage without a suitable cohort.
sections.Return to sport or work:
Criteria

Use criteria rather than a calendar date alone. The patient should have no concerning skin/neurovascular findings, minimal or acceptable pain, functional active ROM, confidence with the required tasks, and adequate strength/endurance and sport-specific tolerance. For post-operative cases, surgeon clearance and protection of the reconstruction take precedence.

Testing battery

  • Compare active ROM and symptom response with the opposite side.
  • Assess cuff and scapular strength/endurance using reproducible dynamometry or standardised resistance testing where available.
  • Progress closed-chain loading (wall/incline/floor push-up), controlled pressing, pulling and lifting relevant to work/sport.
  • Use sport-specific drills: throwing, swimming strokes, tackling/contact preparation, cycling position or falls-risk exposure as relevant.
  • Assess confidence, apprehension and ability to tolerate a full training session before unrestricted return.

Graded return plan

  1. Daily activities and light modified work.
  2. Non-contact conditioning and low-load upper-limb exercises.
  3. Progressive resistance and controlled sport-specific skills.
  4. Full training without contact, then controlled contact exposure where relevant.
  5. Unrestricted training and competition after successful completion of the preceding stages.

Limb symmetry and contact-sport thresholds

No validated ACJ-specific limb-symmetry threshold or contact-sport return battery was identified. Do not present a generic 90% symmetry threshold as validated for ACJ injury. In practice, near-symmetry may be a useful comparison, but interpret it alongside absolute capacity, symptoms, sport demands and the patient's pre-injury level. Contact athletes require progressive exposure to collision, falling and protective arm reactions; exact thresholds remain an evidence gap.10
sections.Clinical pearls & exam traps:
Clinical pearls

  • A visible step deformity supports ACJ separation but does not tell you the patient's functional prognosis.
  • Rockwood classification is based on direction and magnitude of displacement and associated soft-tissue disruption, not pain severity.
  • Always inspect skin and screen distal neurovascular status after significant trauma.
  • Cross-body adduction, Paxinos and O'Brien tests reproduce symptoms but have limited standalone diagnostic value.
  • For many type III injuries, a structured non-operative trial is reasonable; discuss surgery individually rather than treating the X-ray.

Common exam traps

  • Calling an ACJ separation a glenohumeral dislocation.
  • Assuming a positive O'Brien test confirms ACJ pathology or a SLAP lesion.
  • Failing to consider distal clavicle fracture or posterior sternoclavicular displacement.
  • Using weighted radiographs routinely or claiming they are essential to grade every injury.
  • Giving a fixed return-to-sport date without functional criteria.
  • Promising that rehabilitation will remove the cosmetic bump.

Viva questions

  1. How would you distinguish an ACJ injury from a glenohumeral dislocation?
    ACJ injury produces focal superior shoulder pain/tenderness and may cause distal clavicle prominence; glenohumeral dislocation produces altered glenohumeral contour and marked restriction of shoulder movement. Confirm suspected structural injury with appropriate medical assessment and imaging.
  2. What structures are disrupted in a type III injury?
    The AC capsuloligamentous complex and both CC ligaments (conoid and trapezoid) are disrupted, producing superior displacement of the distal clavicle; the deltotrapezial fascia is more extensively compromised in type V.
  3. Which special test would you use?
    I would not rely on one test. I would assess focal tenderness, mechanism, observation and symptom reproduction with cross-body adduction/Paxinos or O'Brien as appropriate, recognising their limited diagnostic accuracy.
  4. How would you manage a type III injury?
    After excluding fracture, skin compromise and neurovascular injury, discuss a non-operative pathway for many patients: short-term comfort sling, early protected movement, progressive scapular/cuff strengthening and graded functional loading. Refer for specialist discussion if persistent symptoms, instability or high-demand considerations warrant it.
  5. When can an athlete return to contact sport?
    When pain is acceptable, ROM and strength/endurance meet the athlete's task demands, confidence is restored, sport-specific drills and controlled contact are tolerated, and any surgical restrictions are cleared. There is no validated universal ACJ-specific time or symmetry threshold.
sections.Evidence summary:
Clinical practice guideline

No dedicated, high-quality Australian clinical practice guideline for isolated ACJ sprain/separation was identified in the sources reviewed. Local assessment, referral and prescribing decisions should follow current Australian professional standards and the treating service's pathways.

Where the evidence is thin

Evidence is weakest for validated acute special-test accuracy, optimal exercise dose and progression, ACJ-specific MCID/MDC values, taping/bracing effectiveness, injection timing, contact-sport clearance criteria and the frequency of residual symptoms at one year. Many diagnostic estimates come from chronic or non-traumatic populations, while rehabilitation recommendations rely heavily on small studies, narrative reviews and variable protocols. Surgical trials also compare particular techniques rather than every contemporary reconstruction. Treat the page as an evidence-informed clinical framework, not a substitute for individual assessment or specialist advice.
